title: Anthropic's Claude Agents Close 186 Deals Without Human Approval
summary:
The efficiency of an AI model can lead to uneven pricing in autonomous markets without the losing party ever realizing they were disadvantaged. In an internal trial called Project Deal, 69 Anthropic employees used Claude agents to close 186 deals for goods and services worth over $4,000 without any human approval. While Opus agents sold identical items for $2.68 more and bought them for $2.45 less than Haiku agents, users on both sides rated the fairness of the deals almost identically at 4.06 and 4.05 on a 7 point scale.

Anthropic is consulting law firms to build negotiating ethics into agents designed to haggle, settle disputes and negotiate pay on behalf of humans. A separate experiment, Project Swap, found that the model's power mattered more than its instructions; switching from the Haiku to the Opus model increased gains by 0.12, while giving the agent 'ruthless' instructions only increased gains by 0.02.

Anthropic wants those norms for Claude agents that will haggle, settle disputes and negotiate pay against other people’s agents.

In Project Deal, 69 employees’ Claude agents closed 186 deals worth just over $4,000 with no human approving any trade.

Opus agents sold identical items for $2.68 more and bought them for $2.45 less than Haiku agents, yet Haiku users rated their deals as fair as Opus users did, 4.06 versus 4.05 on a 7-point scale.

That blindness is the uncomfortable result: if agent quality varies in real markets, people on the losing side may never learn they paid more.

Project Swap then showed that instructions matter far less than the model, with ruthless agents gaining only 0.02 while a switch from Haiku to Opus gained 0.12.
